The wave impedance of free space (air) is approximately 377 ohms.
Low reflection absorbers aim to reduce reflections from dissipative materials at radar frequencies (cm and mm wavelengths).
Reflection factor r is defined as r = (W - Z0) / (W + Z0), where W is absorber input impedance and Z0 is free space impedance.
Good absorbers have reflection factor magnitude |r| less than 0.1 over their effective frequency bandwidth.
Wide-band absorbers typically use geometric gradual transitions like wedge or pyramid shapes and are relatively thick.
Narrow-band absorbers use resonant structures such as quarter-wave layers, dipoles, or slotted foils and are thinner.
The angle of incidence and polarization direction affect the reflection factor and must be considered in absorber design.
Electromagnetic absorbers share principles with acoustical absorbers, including impedance matching and resonant absorption.
Multi-layer absorbers with thin layers create gradual impedance transitions and reduce reflections by interference.
Homogeneous absorbers rely on intrinsic material losses without spatial impedance matching.
The reflection factor depends on both amplitude and phase of the input impedance relative to free space impedance.
Nonreflecting rooms (anechoic chambers) use wide-band absorbers to simulate free-space conditions for electromagnetic measurements.
Back-scatter or radar reflection refers to power reflected back toward the source, important in stealth applications.
Resonant absorbers exhibit frequency-dependent reflection minima due to interference between waves reflected from multiple planes.
Porous materials and wedge-shaped absorbers are effective for wide-band acoustic and electromagnetic absorption.
The quarter-wave (λ/4) spacing between absorbing layers and metal backing can create destructive interference to reduce reflection.
Absorbers can be designed to match impedance at specific incidence angles for one polarization but not necessarily both.
The thickness of absorbers for longer wavelengths (meters) becomes impractically large, limiting their use.
Measurement techniques include free-space and reverberation chamber methods to characterize absorber reflection and absorption.
The paper provides a systematic classification of absorbers based on spatial distribution and structure: inhomogeneous, resonant, and homogeneous.
